title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Ecology — 2021
origin: curated NEB-pattern set filling the 2021 gap for class-11 ecology

questions.question: Define ecological succession. Distinguish primary from secondary succession with one example each, and name the stable final community.
questions.solution:
Succession is the gradual, directional replacement of one community by another in an area over time, driven by the organisms themselves modifying the environment.
Primary succession starts on a bare, lifeless surface with no soil — e.g. lichens and mosses colonising bare volcanic rock, slowly building soil for larger plants.
Secondary succession restarts where a community was disturbed but soil remains — e.g. a forest regrowing after a fire or abandoned farmland returning to woodland; it is much faster.
The stable end-stage community in equilibrium with the climate is the climax community.

questions.question: What is the 10% law of energy flow? A food chain is: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. If grass traps $20{,}000\,\mathrm{kJ}$, how much energy reaches the snake?
questions.solution:
Lindeman's 10% law: only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level transfers to the next; ~90% is lost as heat through respiration, movement and waste.
Grass (producer): $20{,}000\,\mathrm{kJ}$ → grasshopper: 10% = $2{,}000\,\mathrm{kJ}$ → frog: $200\,\mathrm{kJ}$ → snake: $20\,\mathrm{kJ}$. This repeated 90% loss is why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels and why top carnivores are few.

questions.question: In a pyramid of biomass in a pond ecosystem, which level forms the base and why is the pyramid inverted there?
questions.solution: Producers (phytoplankton) form the base. The pyramid is inverted because the standing crop of tiny, short-lived phytoplankton at any moment weighs less than the zooplankton and fish it supports — the producers reproduce so fast that a small biomass sustains a larger consumer biomass. (Pyramids of energy are never inverted; only biomass and number can be.)
